query.original_query: interpretability of foundation models representing thermodynamic laws and conservation laws in physics

sub_queries.semantic_query: mechanistic interpretability of foundation models representing physical laws, thermodynamics, conservation laws, encoding physics knowledge in neural network circuits and features
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how foundation models encode physical laws, specifically thermodynamics and conservation principles, within their internal representations. Using sparse autoencoders and causal tracing, we analyze the residual stream and MLP layers of a large language model to localize features corresponding to energy conservation, entropy, and thermodynamic equilibrium. Our analysis reveals monosemantic features that activate reliably for physical scenarios involving isolated systems and heat transfer, while other features exhibit polysemantic behavior, conflating thermodynamic concepts with unrelated statistical mechanics. Activation patching experiments demonstrate that intervening on these features causally alters the model’s predictions on physics reasoning tasks, confirming their functional role. We further find that feature splitting occurs across multiple attention heads, suggesting distributed encoding of conservation laws. Reconstruction fidelity of these physics features correlates with the model’s accuracy on textbook thermodynamics problems. Results show that foundation models develop sparse, interpretable circuits for representing fundamental physical constraints, though superposition remains prevalent for more abstract thermodynamic quantities. Our findings contribute to understanding how scientific knowledge is organized in large neural networks.

sub_queries.domain: physics education / cognitive science of physics
sub_queries.semantic_query: how humans learn and represent thermodynamic laws and conservation laws, physics conceptual understanding, mental models of physics principles in education and cognitive science
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated how students develop mental models of the first and second laws of thermodynamics, focusing on the conceptual distinction between energy conservation and entropy increase. Using the Thermodynamic Concept Inventory and semi-structured clinical interviews, we measured reasoning patterns among undergraduate engineering and physics majors before and after a semester of instruction. Results indicate that learners frequently conflate energy conservation with the idea that energy is "used up," a persistent alternative framework resistant to traditional instruction. Findings support the hypothesis that novices construct a single, undifferentiated "resource" model for energy, rather than separate models for conservation and degradation. Furthermore, responses to problems involving cyclic processes revealed that many students apply a linear, input-output causal schema to thermodynamic systems, even when such reasoning violates the state-function nature of entropy. These results align with prior work in cognitive science of physics showing that domain-general heuristics, such as teleological thinking, interfere with the acquisition of formal thermodynamic principles. Implications for curriculum design targeting conceptual change are discussed.

papers.title: Deep learning of thermodynamic laws from microscopic dynamics
papers.research_question: Can a deep neural network learn macroscopic thermodynamic laws purely from microscopic data, and behave like a Lieb–Yngvason machine that encodes thermodynamic axioms?
papers.core_contribution: A deep neural network can learn macroscopic thermodynamic laws, specifically the axioms of thermodynamics and an entropy representation, purely from microscopic data without prior thermodynamic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: A DNN can learn thermodynamic laws from microscopic data, opening a pathway to data-driven discovery of macroscopic physics.
papers.key_findings:
The trained DNN induces an order relation between states that satisfies the axioms of thermodynamics.
The internal representation ˜S learned by the DNN acts as an entropy, matching the van der Waals entropy formula.
The DNN can behave as a Lieb–Yngvason machine, which encodes thermodynamic order.
The approach demonstrates that machine learning can discover emergent physical laws from microscopic data.
The success depends on data preparation, task design, and network architecture.
papers.limitation:
The demonstration is on a gas system with short-range repulsive interactions; generality to other systems is not established.
The DNN was not designed to compare states with different particle numbers (states with different N are incomparable).
The study focused on densities below the phase transition; phase transitions or solid phases might pose challenges.
future_direction: Investigate wider class of systems (e.g., Lennard-Jones particles, anharmonic lattice models).
Extend to quantum systems.
Examine systems with phase transitions.
papers.abstract: We numerically show that a deep neural network (DNN) can learn macroscopic thermodynamic laws purely from microscopic data. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we generate the data of snapshot images of gas particles undergoing adiabatic processes. We train a DNN to determine the temporal order of input image pairs. We observe that the trained network induces an order relation between states consistent with adiabatic accessibility, satisfying the axioms of thermodynamics. Furthermore, the internal representation learned by the DNN acts as an entropy. These results suggest that machine learning can discover emergent physical laws that are valid at scales far larger than those of the underlying constituents---opening a pathway to data-driven discovery of macroscopic physics.

papers.title: Physical Symmetries Embedded in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can physical constraints (such as symmetries and conservation laws) be embedded into neural network architectures to guarantee that predictions obey known physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture (hub layer) that embeds physical constraints (symmetries and conservation laws) exactly into the network structure, guaranteeing that predictions satisfy the underlying physics without the need for explicit regularization terms.
papers.conclusion: Embedding physical constraints into neural networks via hub layers improves predictive power, training efficiency, and robustness, and is crucial for reliable predictions in data-scarce regimes.
papers.key_findings:
A hub layer can enforce even/odd symmetry in regression tasks, outperforming standard MLPs in preserving symmetry while fitting noisy data.
For energy-conserving regression, a hub layer that corrects the MLP prediction using Hamiltonian dynamics ensures energy conservation and closed phase-space trajectories.
An unsupervised symplectic neural network, designed by embedding Hamilton's equations, conserves energy when solving differential equations and converges faster than a standard MLP.
future_direction: Embed other important symmetries into neural networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are a central technique in machine learning. Recent years have seen a wave of interest in applying neural networks to physical systems for which the governing dynamics are known and expressed through differential equations. Two fundamental challenges facing the development of neural networks in physics applications is their lack of interpretability and their physics-agnostic design. The focus of the present work is to embed physical constraints into the structure of the neural network to address the second fundamental challenge. By constraining tunable parameters (such as weights and biases) and adding special layers to the network, the desired constraints are guaranteed to be satisfied without the need for explicit regularization terms. This is demonstrated on upervised and unsupervised networks for two basic symmetries: even/odd symmetry of a function and energy conservation. In the supervised case, the network with embedded constraints is shown to perform well on regression problems while simultaneously obeying the desired constraints whereas a traditional network fits the data but violates the underlying constraints. Finally, a new unsupervised neural network is proposed that guarantees energy conservation through an embedded symplectic structure. The symplectic neural network is used to solve a system of energy-conserving differential equations and out-performs an unsupervised, non-symplectic neural network.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Operationally meaningful representations of physical systems in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks to learn operationally meaningful representations of physical systems that separate parameters relevant for different experimental settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture that learns operationally meaningful representations of physical systems by imposing a communication efficiency criterion between agents, leading to disentangled parameters that correspond to physically relevant quantities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed architecture can learn operationally meaningful representations that separate physically relevant parameters, and it can be combined with reinforcement learning for interactive settings.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture can separate local parameters from interaction parameters in classical charged particle systems.
It can separate local qubit parameters from quantum correlation parameters in two-qubit systems.
The method can be combined with reinforcement learning to learn representations in interactive scenarios.
future_direction: Combining the method with reinforcement learning for more complex environments.
Exploring other operational criteria for representation learning.
papers.abstract: Abstract To make progress in science, we often build abstract representations of physical systems that meaningfully encode information about the systems. Such representations ignore redundant features and treat parameters such as velocity and position separately because they can be useful for making statements about different experimental settings. Here, we capture this notion by formally defining the concept of operationally meaningful representations. We present an autoencoder architecture with attention mechanism that can generate such representations and demonstrate it on examples involving both classical and quantum physics. For instance, our architecture finds a compact representation of an arbitrary two-qubit system that separates local parameters from parameters describing quantum correlations.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: TIME: A Transparent, Interpretable, Model-Adaptive and Explainable Neural Network for Dynamic Physical Processes
papers.research_question: Can we recover an invariant structure (PDE) from dense space-time observations, detect anomalies, and make the network interpretable and transparent?
papers.core_contribution: A low-weight, fully convolutional encoder-decoder network that learns interpretable representations of PDEs from space-time data, with transparency and explainability.
papers.conclusion: The TIME network is effective for learning PDE representations and provides interpretability and explainability, allowing modelers to verify the network's workings against their domain knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The network can learn PDE kernels that approximate differential operators.
Network design (depth and number of kernels) affects interpretability and accuracy.
The network is robust to scaling and can detect missing data as anomalies in activation maps.
A compact representation (appropriate depth and kernel count) performs best while maintaining interpretability.
High-weight representations are redundant and impact interpretability.
future_direction: Imbibe complicated processes with additional domain constraints.
papers.abstract: Partial Differential Equations are infinite dimensional encoded representations of physical processes. However, imbibing multiple observation data towards a coupled representation presents significant challenges. We present a fully convolutional architecture that captures the invariant structure of the domain to reconstruct the observable system. The proposed architecture is significantly low-weight compared to other networks for such problems. Our intent is to learn coupled dynamic processes interpreted as deviations from true kernels representing isolated processes for model-adaptivity. Experimental analysis shows that our architecture is robust and transparent in capturing process kernels and system anomalies. We also show that high weights representation is not only redundant but also impacts network interpretability. Our design is guided by domain knowledge, with isolated process representations serving as ground truths for verification. These allow us to identify redundant kernels and their manifestations in activation maps to guide better designs that are both interpretable and explainable unlike traditional deep-nets.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Neural Networks Discover Physical Principles from Observation with an Intuitive World Model
papers.research_question: Can neural networks discover and explain physical principles (such as Newton's laws and Coulomb's law) from raw visual observations, similar to how humans learn intuitive physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Intuitive World Model (IWM), a neural network that learns physical principles (e.g., Newton's laws, Coulomb's law) from raw video data without built-in physics engines, and can provide explicit explanations and perform counterfactual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the Intuitive World Model (IWM) can learn physical principles from visual observation, providing explicit explanations and counterfactual reasoning, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
IWM achieves state-of-the-art performance on causal reasoning tasks (factual, predictive, counterfactual) on the ComPhy dataset.
IWM learns interpretable physical principles, as shown by its ability to generate force diagrams and explain physical events.
The hierarchical learning paradigm enables IWM to progressively learn appearance, velocity, mass, and charge representations.
IWM can perform counterfactual imagination by manipulating inferred physical properties (mass, charge) and generating plausible alternative scenarios.
The learned causal modules capture relationships analogous to Newton's laws and Coulomb's law, as demonstrated by sensitivity analysis.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Humans readily grasp physical principles via visual observation, underpinning our ability to model the world and reason about events. In contrast, AI systems often fail to extract consistent physical rules from video, relying on black-box mechanisms that produce implausible outcomes. We introduce the Intuitive World Model (IWM), designed to learn physical principles directly from vision, mimicking human intuition. Drawing inspiration from developmental psychology, IWM utilizes a modular architecture to decompose interactions into force-based dynamics. Through observing objects collide and interact via charges, it identifies intrinsic properties like mass and charge and learns representations analogous to Newton's and Coulomb's laws. This paradigm uniquely allows neural networks to provide explicit explanations for physical phenomena and conduct counterfactual reasoning consistent with learned physical laws. Our work demonstrates that a developmentally-inspired approach empowers AI to acquire explicit, interpretable physical knowledge from observation, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: GINN-KAN: Interpretability pipelining with applications in Physics Informed Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we create an interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN to overcome their individual limitations and be effectively applied to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GINN-KAN, a novel interpretable neural network that combines the strengths of GINN and KAN, and demonstrates its application to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), creating interpretable PINNs that outperform black-box networks.
papers.conclusion: GINN-KAN represents a significant step forward in developing interpretable neural networks, offering a promising balance between interpretability and performance, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing machine learning frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets.
GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform traditional PINNs with black-box networks on 15 different partial differential equations.
GINN struggles to learn non-Laurent polynomial (non-LP) equations, while KAN struggles to learn equations containing multiplicative terms.
GINN-KAN combines the strengths of both GINN and KAN, performing well on both LP and non-LP equations and on equations with multiplications.
GINN-KAN can be trained using backpropagation and integrated into existing machine learning pipelines with minimal adjustments.
papers.limitation: GINN-KAN is restricted to inputs with positive values, a limitation inherited from GINN.
future_direction: Explore more robust architectures that maintain interpretability while overcoming the positive input limitation.
Develop better regularization techniques to enable GINN-KAN to accurately discover concise ground truth equations.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful function approximators, yet their ``black-box" nature often renders them opaque and difficult to interpret. While many post-hoc explanation methods exist, they typically fail to capture the underlying reasoning processes of the networks. A truly interpretable neural network would be trained similarly to conventional models using techniques such as backpropagation, but additionally provide insights into the learned input-output relationships. In this work, we introduce the concept of interpretability pipelineing, to incorporate multiple interpretability techniques to outperform each individual technique. To this end, we first evaluate several architectures that promise such interpretability, with a particular focus on two recent models selected for their potential to incorporate interpretability into standard neural network architectures while still leveraging backpropagation: the Growing Interpretable Neural Network (GINN) and Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN). We analyze the limitations and strengths of each and introduce a novel interpretable neural network GINN-KAN that synthesizes the advantages of both models. When tested on the Feynman symbolic regression benchmark datasets, GINN-KAN outperforms both GINN and KAN. To highlight the capabilities and the generalizability of this approach, we position GINN-KAN as an alternative to conventional black-box networks in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). We expect this to have far-reaching implications in the application of deep learning pipelines in the natural sciences. Our experiments with this interpretable PINN on 15 different partial differential equations demonstrate that GINN-KAN augmented PINNs outperform PINNs with black-box networks in solving differential equations and surpass the capabilities of both GINN and KAN.

papers.title: Identification of state functions by physically-guided neural networks with physically-meaningful internal layers
papers.research_question: How to predict the input-output relation in a physical system while fulfilling physical constraints, and how to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Physically-Guided Neural Networks with Internal Variables (PGNNIV), a method that integrates physical constraints into neural networks to predict system behavior and infer internal state variables, showing improved convergence, data efficiency, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.conclusion: PGNNIV is a promising framework that combines the predictive power of neural networks with physical interpretability, and shows advantages over standard neural networks in terms of convergence, data needs, noise filtering, and extrapolation.
papers.key_findings:
The method accelerates the training process.
It reduces the amount of data required for similar accuracy.
It filters noise in experimental data.
It provides improved extrapolation capacity.
It allows obtaining internal state variables without additional assumptions.
papers.limitation:
For deep neural models, large and varied data are needed.
Defining successful network topology and hyperparameters is complex and time-consuming.
Predictions may not be as accurate as using full prescribed mathematical models.
papers.abstract: Substitution of well-grounded theoretical models by data-driven predictions is not as simple in engineering and sciences as it is in social and economic fields. Scientific problems suffer most times from paucity of data, while they may involve a large number of variables and parameters that interact in complex and non-stationary ways, obeying certain physical laws. Moreover, a physically-based model is not only useful for making predictions, but to gain knowledge by the interpretation of its structure, parameters, and mathematical properties. The solution to these shortcomings seems to be the seamless blending of the tremendous predictive power of the data-driven approach with the scientific consistency and interpretability of physically-based models. We use here the concept of physically-constrained neural networks (PCNN) to predict the input-output relation in a physical system, while, at the same time fulfilling the physical constraints. With this goal, the internal hidden state variables of the system are associated with a set of internal neuron layers, whose values are constrained by known physical relations, as well as any additional knowledge on the system. Furthermore, when having enough data, it is possible to infer knowledge about the internal structure of the system and, if parameterized, to predict the state parameters for a particular input-output relation. We show that this approach, besides getting physically-based predictions, accelerates the training process, reduces the amount of data required to get similar accuracy, filters partly the intrinsic noise in the experimental data and provides improved extrapolation capacity.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Neural Thermodynamics: Entropic Forces in Deep and Universal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How do entropic forces arising from stochasticity and discrete-time updates in SGD govern representation learning and lead to emergent phenomena such as universal representation alignment and gradient balance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an entropic-force theory for SGD dynamics, showing that entropic forces break continuous parameter symmetries and lead to gradient balance phenomena and universal representation alignment.
papers.conclusion: Entropic forces and symmetry breaking unify various emergent phenomena in deep learning, such as progressive sharpening and universal representation alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Entropic forces break continuous parameter symmetries but preserve discrete ones.
Gradient balance (equipartition) emerges between layers and neurons due to entropic forces.
Entropic forces explain progressive sharpening and flattening of the loss landscape during training.
Entropic forces lead to universal representation alignment, providing a proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Weight decay breaks the universal alignment, showing a trade-off between gradient balance and weight balance.
papers.limitation: The theory applies to SGD with small learning rates and weight decay; extensions to adaptive optimizers and large learning rates are future work.
future_direction: Extending the theory to adaptive optimizers and large learning rates.
Exploring the role of discrete symmetries.
Investigating the connection to biological learning.
papers.abstract: With the rapid discovery of emergent phenomena in deep learning and large language models, understanding their cause has become an urgent need. Here, we propose a rigorous entropic-force theory for understanding the learning dynamics of neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. Building on the theory of parameter symmetries and an entropic loss landscape, we show that representation learning is crucially governed by emergent entropic forces arising from stochasticity and discrete-time updates. These forces systematically break continuous parameter symmetries and preserve discrete ones, leading to a series of gradient balance phenomena that resemble the equipartition property of thermal systems. These phenomena, in turn, (a) explain the universal alignment of neural representations between AI models and lead to a proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, and (b) reconcile the seemingly contradictory observations of sharpness- and flatness-seeking behavior of deep learning optimization. Our theory and experiments demonstrate that a combination of entropic forces and symmetry breaking is key to understanding emergent phenomena in deep learning.

papers.title: Inducing Causal World Models in LLMs for Zero-Shot Physical Reasoning
