papers.research_question: How can we induce a causal world model in Large Language Models to improve zero-shot physical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal World Model Induction (CWMI) framework, which augments a frozen LLM with a trainable Causal Physics Module and a Causal Intervention Loss to learn cause-and-effect relationships, significantly improving zero-shot physical reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Inducing an explicit causal world model within an LLM via the CWMI framework is a critical and effective step towards building AI systems with robust, generalizable physical reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CWMI achieves 89.4% zero-shot accuracy on PIQA, outperforming Llama 3 8B (74.2%) and GPT-4 (85.5%).
On the novel PhysiCa-Bench, CWMI achieves 94.1% accuracy, 87.6% Causal Consistency Score, and a low Future State Prediction Error (MSE 0.08).
Ablation studies show the Causal Intervention Loss is critical for causal consistency, and the State Prediction Loss is necessary for grounding predictions in physical reality.
The two-component architecture (frozen LLM + trainable CPM) is more effective than fine-tuning the LLM directly, validating the modular design.
Performance scales with CPM capacity, plateauing at around 256M parameters for the rigid-body dynamics in the benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Struggles with complex multi-object interactions (e.g., a pile of falling blocks).
Cannot handle non-rigid and fluid dynamics, as training was on rigid-body physics.
Fails when key physical properties are not explicitly stated or strongly implied in the text (e.g., implicit understanding that a feather has high air resistance).
future_direction: Architectural enhancements to the CPM, such as adopting graph neural networks for multi-object tracking.
Incorporating physics-informed neural network techniques for continuous fields like fluids.
Integrating more sophisticated 3D visual representations.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their advanced linguistic capabilities, fundamentally lack an intuitive understanding of physical dynamics, which limits their effectiveness in real-world scenarios that require causal reasoning. In this paper, we introduce Causal World Model Induction (CWMI), a novel framework designed to embed an explicit model of causal physics within an LLM. Our approach incorporates a dedicated Causal Physics Module (CPM) and a new training objective called Causal Intervention Loss, encouraging the model to learn cause-and-effect relationships from multimodal data. By training the model to predict the outcomes of hypothetical interventions instead of merely capturing statistical correlations, CWMI develops a robust internal representation of physical laws. Experimental results show that CWMI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLMs on zero-shot physical reasoning tasks, including the PIQA benchmark and our newly proposed PhysiCa-Bench dataset. These findings demonstrate that inducing a causal world model is a critical step toward more reliable and generalizable AI systems.

papers.title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics
papers.research_question: How does the function space of training data affect the generalization of machine learning models when learning linear differential equations, and can learned models be interpreted in terms of Green's functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization in learning spatial physics depends critically on the function space of the training data, and introduces a cross-validation technique and a mechanistic interpretability lens based on extracting Green's functions from learned models.
papers.conclusion: Learning spatially dependent problems is limited by the underlying function space of the training data, and careful data selection and cross-validation are needed; different model classes exhibit opposing generalization behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Learned parameters in finite difference models converge with error depending on grid spacing and polynomial order of data.
Linear models only converge to a projection of the true operator onto the subspace of the training data, limiting out-of-distribution generalization.
Deep models and SciML models (DeepONet, Neural Operator) do not always generalize out-of-distribution.
Physics-informed losses (PINNs, PI-DeepONet) suffer from the same subspace limitation as black-box models.
Green's function operators can be extracted from black-box models when they generalize effectively across test domains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis requires a priori knowledge of how the dataset was constructed.
Real-world data collection has inherent limitations that may hinder discovering unknown physics.
future_direction: Develop new methods capable of discovering the underlying subspace of the data to compensate for limitations.
Use cross-set generalization as an evaluation benchmark for future differential equation learning techniques.
papers.abstract: While there are many applications of ML to scientific problems that look promising, visuals can be deceiving. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the function space of the data is critical to the generalization of the model. A similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models, including physics-specific techniques. Counterintuitively, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green's function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, which can serve as a benchmark.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: The Dynamics of Neural Populations Capture the Laws of the Mind
papers.research_question: What would it mean to explain the mind in neural terms? The paper investigates how the dynamics of neural populations can capture the laws of the mind.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that neural population dynamics, described as attractor states in low-dimensional feature spaces, form a privileged level of description for cognition, where macroscopic patterns enslave microscopic neural activity, and that networks of such dynamics constitute neural cognitive architectures.
papers.conclusion: The dynamics of neural populations form a privileged level of description at which the laws of behavior and cognition manifest themselves, and this level cannot be eliminated by reduction to a more microscopic level.
papers.key_findings:
Neural populations are a privileged level of description to understand cognition and behavior.
Neural dynamics at the population level generate stable attractor states that serve as representations.
Cognition unfolds as sequences of stable neural states are autonomously generated by neural dynamical systems that go through instabilities.
Networks of neural dynamics constitute neural cognitive architectures that enable increasingly complex forms of cognition.
The reduction of mind to neural mechanisms should follow the non-equilibrium physics metaphor, where macroscopic neural states enslave microscopic neural activity.
papers.limitation:
The separation of scales between macroscopic neural dynamics and microscopic neural activity might be broken by complex nonlinear processes that reach across spatial and temporal scales.
The paper does not cover how macroscopic neural dynamics are re-shaped by experience through neural mechanisms of learning.
future_direction: Address how macroscopic neural dynamics are re-shaped by experience through neural mechanisms of learning.
Explore scale-free theories that avoid reductive elimination of the macroscopic scale.
papers.abstract: What would it mean to explain the mind in neural terms? Neural accounts of the mind are often sought in a reductionistic spirit in which neural mechanisms explain cognition. Because an individual's thoughts and behaviors are not reproducible without careful control of task, stimulus, and behavioral history, laws of the mind are the currency of psychology. Reduction may thus have to take the form familiar from physics: deriving macroscopic laws from microscopic laws. I argue that the metaphor of reduction from non-equilibrium physics may be the most appropriate. Macroscopic patterns of neural activity, which cause behavior and thought, are slow dynamical variables that dominate the fast microscopic dynamics of individual neurons and synapses. I outline a theoretical framework in which strongly recurrent neural networks, described by neural dynamics, generate neural representations as attractor states that are embedded in low-dimensional feature spaces. Instabilities of these states are instrumental in decision-making and the generation of sequences of mental states that are the basis for higher cognition. Networks of such neural population dynamics form neural cognitive architectures that capture the laws of the mind.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy
papers.research_question: How can philosophy contribute to mechanistic interpretability? The paper investigates three open problems in MI and how philosophy can help.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy to clarify its concepts, refine its methods, and assess the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that philosophy is deeply relevant to mechanistic interpretability and invites deeper interdisciplinary collaboration that is technically informed and philosophically grounded.
papers.key_findings:
Philosophy can help in decomposing networks into interpretable parts by providing conceptual tools from mechanistic explanation and challenging the assumption of a single true decomposition.
Philosophy can clarify the concept of 'features' in AI systems by distinguishing between vehicles and content of representations, refining experimental approaches, and suggesting new lines of investigation.
Philosophy can help in detecting deceptive behavior by clarifying concepts like lying and deception, guiding the search for AI beliefs, and drawing ethical and normative boundaries.
future_direction: Deeper interdisciplinary collaboration between philosophy and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to explain how neural networks work by uncovering their underlying causal mechanisms. As the field grows in influence, it is increasingly important to examine not just models themselves, but the assumptions, concepts and explanatory strategies implicit in MI research. We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy: not as an afterthought, but as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and assessing the epistemic and ethical stakes of interpreting AI systems. Taking three open problems from the MI literature as examples, this position paper illustrates the value philosophy can add to MI research, and outlines a path toward deeper interdisciplinary dialogue.

papers.title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to derive compact formal guarantees on model performance? Does more compact proof require and provide more mechanistic understanding, and does more faithful understanding lead to tighter bounds?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact formal proofs of model performance, and shows that more compact proofs require more mechanistic understanding and that more faithful understanding leads to tighter bounds.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can be used to generate compact proofs of model performance, but compounding structureless errors pose a challenge that future work must address.
papers.key_findings:
Shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding.
More faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds.
Compounding structureless errors is a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.
papers.limitation:
Compounding structureless errors pose a challenge for generating compact proofs.
The approach is demonstrated only on a simple toy setting (Max-of-K).
future_direction: Addressing the challenge of compounding structureless errors in generating compact proofs.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and models.
papers.abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance. We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-K, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of K. We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models. Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding. Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds. We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs. Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: How can we combine deep learning and symbolic regression to extract interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, specifically Graph Neural Networks, to discover physical laws and improve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that combines deep learning (specifically Graph Neural Networks with strong inductive biases) and symbolic regression to distill interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, enabling the discovery of physical laws and improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully distills symbolic, interpretable models from Graph Neural Networks, recovers known physical laws, discovers new formulas in cosmology, and improves generalization, offering a promising direction for interpreting deep learning models and advancing scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract known physical equations (e.g., force laws and Hamiltonians) from the learned representations of Graph Neural Networks.
Applied to a cosmology dataset, the framework discovered a new analytic formula for predicting dark matter halo concentration from the mass distribution of nearby structures.
The extracted symbolic expressions generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the original Graph Neural Network model.
The framework demonstrates that neural networks can learn representations that are linear transformations of true physical quantities (e.g., forces) when appropriate inductive biases are applied.
The approach offers a pathway to interpret neural networks and discover novel physical principles from the representations they learn.
future_direction: Extending the framework to gridded PDE data using existing symbolic regression packages for PDEs.
Using other symbolic regression packages (e.g., PySR, grammar-based methods) as drop-in replacements for eureqa in the framework.
papers.abstract: We develop a general approach to distill symbolic representations of a learned deep model by introducing strong inductive biases. We focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The technique works as follows: we first encourage sparse latent representations when we train a GNN in a supervised setting, then we apply symbolic regression to components of the learned model to extract explicit physical relations. We find the correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, can be extracted from the neural network. We then apply our method to a non-trivial cosmology example-a detailed dark matter simulation-and discover a new analytic formula which can predict the concentration of dark matter from the mass distribution of nearby cosmic structures. The symbolic expressions extracted from the GNN using our technique also generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the GNN itself. Our approach offers alternative directions for interpreting neural networks and discovering novel physical principles from the representations they learn.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Discovering symmetry invariants and conserved quantities by interpreting siamese neural networks
papers.research_question: Can Siamese Neural Networks learn symmetry invariants and conserved quantities in physical systems, and can they be interpreted to reveal these quantities without prior knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces interpretable Siamese Neural Networks to theoretical physics and shows they can learn and reveal symmetry invariants and conserved quantities without prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: SNNs are a useful tool in theoretical physics and can be interpreted to reveal physical invariants, challenging the black box nature of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
SNNs learn the spacetime interval in special relativity.
SNNs learn angular momentum and energy in central potential motion.
SNNs learn the two electromagnetic invariants (E·B and |E|^2-|B|^2).
The bottleneck layer of the SNN can be interpreted via polynomial regression to approximate the invariants.
The SNN fails to learn when the invariant is fixed, indicating it relies on that invariant.
future_direction: Upgrade polynomial regression to symbolic regression.
Combine interpretable SNNs with mathematical reasoning tools (solvers or theorem provers).
Apply to quantum error correction or particle tracking at the LHC.
papers.abstract: The authors train a Siamese neural network to decide whether two different descriptions describe the same physical object. The neural network learns to identify the objects by calculating the underlying invariants and conserved quantities.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction provides a solid theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, enabling precise definitions of core concepts and a unified perspective on existing methods, which facilitates rigorous falsification through experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal abstraction theory is generalized to allow for arbitrary mechanism transformations (interventionals), which enables the isolation of quantities distributed across overlapping sets of microvariables.
The core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness are given flexible, mathematically precise definitions within the causal abstraction framework.
A wide range of mechanistic interpretability methods (e.g., activation patching, causal scrubbing, sparse autoencoders, steering) and behavioral interpretability methods (e.g., LIME, integrated gradients) are unified under the common language of causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction provides a theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, the field concerned with providing intelligible algorithms that are faithful simplifications of the known, but opaque low-level details of black box AI models. Our contributions are (1) generalizing the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement (i.e., hard and soft interventions) to arbitrary mechanism transformation (i.e., functionals from old mechanisms to new mechanisms), (2) providing a flexible, yet precise formalization for the core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness, and (3) unifying a variety of mechanistic interpretability methods in the common language of causal abstraction, namely, activation and path patching, causal mediation analysis, causal scrubbing, causal tracing, circuit analysis, concept erasure, sparse autoencoders, differential binary masking, distributed alignment search, and steering.

papers.title: Towards mechanistic understanding in a data-driven weather model: internal activations reveal interpretable physical features
papers.research_question: Whether interpretable abstractions corresponding to physical features are present in the internal representations of data-driven physics models like GraphCast, and if these abstractions are physically consistent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable physical features from the internal activations of the data-driven weather model GraphCast, and that modifying these features leads to physically consistent changes in predictions, offering a window into the model's black-box behavior.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders applied to GraphCast extract highly interpretable physical features, and modifying these features allows probing of the model's internal abstractions, contributing to model trust and potential scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features in GraphCast corresponding to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal/seasonal patterns, precipitation, geographical coding, and sea-ice extent.
Features like sea-ice extent are learned dynamically even though not present in the model's input or output.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are identified, reflecting potential architecture bias.
Sparse probing identifies single features that strongly predict tropical cyclones and atmospheric rivers.
Interventions that modify a tropical cyclone feature lead to interpretable and physically consistent changes in hurricane strength and evolution in the model's predictions.
papers.limitation:
The correlation between sea-ice features and actual ice extent is demonstrated, but a more rigorous causal analysis is needed for a complete account.
Grid-locked features that activate on the model's mesh structure are spurious and potentially undesirable from an interpretability perspective.
ERA5 fields themselves are not in perfect hydrostatic balance, which affects the evaluation of physical consistency.
future_direction: Conduct more rigorous causal analysis of the discovered features.
Build mechanistic accounts for the interaction of features leading to model predictions.
Train specifically sparse models to have interpretable computations.
papers.abstract: Large data-driven physics models like DeepMind's weather model GraphCast have empirically succeeded in parameterizing time operators for complex dynamical systems with an accuracy reaching or in some cases exceeding that of traditional physics-based solvers. Unfortunately, how these data-driven models perform computations is largely unknown and whether their internal representations are interpretable or physically consistent is an open question. Here, we adapt tools from interpretability research in Large Language Models to analyze intermediate computational layers in GraphCast, leveraging sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable features in the neuron space of the model. We uncover distinct features on a wide range of length and time scales that correspond to tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, diurnal and seasonal behavior, large-scale precipitation patterns, specific geographical coding, and sea-ice extent, among others. We further demonstrate how the precise abstraction of these features can be probed via interventions on the prediction steps of the model. As a case study, we sparsely modify a feature corresponding to tropical cyclones in GraphCast and observe interpretable and physically consistent modifications to evolving hurricanes. Such methods offer a window into the black-box behavior of data-driven physics models and are a step towards realizing their potential as trustworthy predictors and scientifically valuable tools for discovery.

papers.title: Encoding and Understanding Astrophysical Information in Large Language Model-Generated Summaries
papers.research_question: To what extent does prompt engineering affect the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities, and how is physics information encoded in text summaries?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can encode physical information from astrophysical text, with structured prompting improving alignment between embeddings and physical quantities, and sparse autoencoders reveal the semantic concepts driving this encoding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can capture, learn, and represent physics concepts in textual data, and prompt engineering enhances the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities. Sparse autoencoders provide insight into the semantic concepts underlying this encoding.
papers.key_findings:
Structured prompts significantly improve the clustering purity of LLM embeddings with respect to physical quantities, with improvements up to 57.5% for variability index.
Sparse autoencoders extract interpretable features from text embeddings that correlate with specific astrophysical properties, such as non-thermal characteristics linked to power-law gamma values.
LLMs infer physical parameters from text descriptions even when numerical values are not explicitly stated, demonstrating an understanding of astrophysical concepts.
Concepts like 'eclipsing binaries' and 'galaxy cluster thermal dynamics' are encoded in the embeddings and associated with physical measurements.
The method allows for visual and quantitative analysis of how physics is encoded in language through t-SNE clustering and SAE feature activation.
future_direction: Expanding the dataset to include more sources
Optimizing prompting with different models
Creating an interface for astronomer validation of possibly anomalous objects
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated the ability to generalize well at many levels across domains, modalities, and even shown in-context learning capabilities. This enables research questions regarding how they can be used to encode physical information that is usually only available from scientific measurements, and loosely encoded in textual descriptions. Using astrophysics as a test bed, we investigate if LLM embeddings can codify physical summary statistics that are obtained from scientific measurements through two main questions: 1) Does prompting play a role on how those quantities are codified by the LLM? and 2) What aspects of language are most important in encoding the physics represented by the measurement? We investigate this using sparse autoencoders that extract interpretable features from the text.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB Shared Task: Improving Circuit Faithfulness via Better Edge Selection
papers.research_question: How to improve circuit faithfulness via better edge selection in circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes bootstrapping, positive-negative ratio (PNR), and integer linear programming (ILP) for edge selection in circuit discovery, improving faithfulness over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Principled edge selection improves faithfulness and enables more robust circuit discovery, despite computational limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Bootstrapping identifies edges with consistent attribution scores, filtering out unstable ones.
Positive-negative ratio (PNR) selection balances positive and negative edges, improving circuit faithfulness.
Integer linear programming (ILP) provides globally optimal edge selection compared to greedy algorithms.
Combinations of these methods outperform baseline approaches across multiple models and tasks on MIB metrics.
papers.limitation:
ILP optimization scales poorly with edge count, limiting applicability to larger models.
Optimal ratio of positive edges varies by models and tasks, requiring task-specific tuning.
Gap between state-of-the-art attribution methods and 'ground truth' edge importance scores limits faithfulness gains from ILP.
papers.abstract: One of the main challenges in mechanistic interpretability is circuit discovery, determining which parts of a model perform a given task. We build on the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB) and propose three key improvements to circuit discovery. First, we use bootstrapping to identify edges with consistent attribution scores. Second, we introduce a simple ratio-based selection strategy to prioritize strong positive-scoring edges, balancing performance and faithfulness. Third, we replace the standard greedy selection with an integer linear programming formulation. Our methods yield more faithful circuits and outperform prior approaches across multiple MIB tasks and models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/MIB-Shared-Task.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Invertible Neural Networks for Understanding Semantics of Invariances of CNN Representations
papers.research_question: How can we understand the semantic concepts and invariances learned by deep neural networks (specifically CNNs) by recovering the invariances and translating the representations into an interpretable form without modifying the original model?
papers.core_contribution: An invertible neural network (INN) approach that recovers the invariances a deep model has learned and bijectively translates the model representation and its invariances into a semantically accessible encoding without compromising the original model's performance.
papers.conclusion: The invertible approach provides a powerful, post-hoc diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering invariances and enabling semantic interpretation without retraining the model.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes representations and their invariances without artifacts, outperforming existing network inversion methods.
Analysis of FaceNet shows that invariances (e.g., to pose) increase with layer depth, while some features (e.g., glasses) remain identity-relevant across layers.
The approach can quantify how much of a semantic concept (e.g., texture vs. shape) is captured by a model's representation, revealing biases like texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
Semantic modifications in the interpretable space correctly alter the original representation and can be visualized, enabling diagnostic probing of model sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Abstract To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black-box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on invertible neural networks (INNs) that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black-box models by enabling post hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Nonlocal Attention Operator: Materializing Hidden Knowledge Towards Interpretable Physics Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we design an attention-based neural operator that simultaneously solves forward and inverse PDE problems, providing interpretability and generalizability to unseen physical systems?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), a novel neural operator architecture that uses an attention-based kernel map to simultaneously solve forward (modeling) and inverse (discovery) PDE problems, offering interpretability and zero-shot generalizability to new physical systems.
papers.conclusion: NAO is an effective neural operator architecture for simultaneously learning forward and inverse PDE solvers from data, providing interpretability through the discovered kernel and zero-shot generalizability to new physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
NAO achieves lower operator and kernel errors compared to discrete and softmax attention variants in forward and inverse PDE tasks.
NAO generalizes to unseen physical systems (zero-shot learning) and across different data resolutions.
The attention mechanism acts as a data-driven regularizer, resolving the ill-posedness of inverse PDE problems by exploring a function space of identifiability.
NAO's kernel map provides interpretability by revealing the hidden physical mechanism (kernel) from data.
NAO outperforms baseline models (Discrete-NAO, Softmax-NAO, NAO-u, AFNO, Autoencoder) in terms of generalizability and accuracy.
papers.limitation: Experiments focus on learning from a small to medium number (<500) of similar physical systems due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Expand the coverage to enable learning across different types of physical systems.
Build a foundation model in scientific machine learning.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent popularity of attention-based neural architectures in core AI fields like natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), their potential in modeling complex physical systems remains under-explored. Learning problems in physical systems are often characterized as discovering operators that map between function spaces based on a few instances of function pairs. This task frequently presents a severely ill-posed PDE inverse problem. In this work, we propose a novel neural operator architecture based on the attention mechanism, which we coin Nonlocal Attention Operator (NAO), and explore its capability towards developing a foundation physical model. In particular, we show that the attention mechanism is equivalent to a double integral operator that enables nonlocal interactions among spatial tokens, with a data-dependent kernel characterizing the inverse mapping from data to the hidden parameter field of the underlying operator. As such, the attention mechanism extracts global prior information from training data generated by multiple systems, and suggests the exploratory space in the form of a nonlinear kernel map. Consequently, NAO can address ill-posedness and rank deficiency in inverse PDE problems by encoding regularization and achieving generalizability. We empirically demonstrate the advantages of NAO over baseline neural models in terms of generalizability to unseen data resolutions and system states. Our work not only suggests a novel neural operator architecture for learning interpretable foundation models of physical systems, but also offers a new perspective towards understanding the attention mechanism. Our code and data accompanying this paper are available at https://github.com/fishmoon1234/NAO.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Talking with the Latents -- how to convert your LLM into an astronomer
papers.research_question: How can domain-specific physical knowledge be introduced into Large Language Models (LLMs) to enable effective reasoning over complex numerical scientific data?
papers.core_contribution: A general framework for using LLMs as interpretable interfaces to scientific latent spaces, enabling a single model to perform diverse tasks through natural language guidance by fusing pre-trained latent physical features with a pre-trained language model via a lightweight adapter and LoRA.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a domain-agnostic framework for aligning scientific foundation models with LLMs, marking a step toward developing scientifically capable and useful LLMs that can serve as interpretable interfaces to scientific latent spaces.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method enables effective reasoning over real scientific data, substantially outperforming strong baselines like Gemini 3 Pro without task-specific fine-tuning.
The model can combine latent information with general physical understanding to predict complex properties (e.g., stellar mass from radius).
The model can be 'steered' by identifying physically meaningful directions in the latent space, allowing for explicit physical manipulation and natural language interpretation.
Performance on complex tasks scales with LLM size, with larger models (Qwen-32B) performing best.
Sparse latent features are crucial for the LLM's successful interpretation, with models using sparse features outperforming those using dense features from a different encoder.
papers.limitation:
Relatively small LLMs and a simple unimodal spectra model were used.
The student model is fundamentally bounded by the quality and biases of the teacher's synthetic descriptions.
The architecture is unidirectional: it can describe data but cannot generate scientific data from text.
future_direction: To fully utilize the potential of this approach, larger LLMs and scientific foundation models should be used.
Enabling a bidirectional flow (generating scientific data from text) requires a different architecture and is a focus of future work.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer unique opportunities for scientific tasks, yet their ability to reason over complex numerical data remains largely unexplored. We propose a simple mechanism to introduce domain-specific physical knowledge into LLMs by fusing pre-trained latent physical features with a pre-trained language model. Our method employs a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework where a large LLM (teacher) generates synthetic question-answer supervision to transfer physical reasoning to a smaller LLM (student). The student is conditioned on latent physical features and trained via a lightweight adapter and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We demonstrate that this approach, applied to models with 1B, 8B, and 32B parameters, enables effective reasoning over real scientific data. Our models substantially outperform strong baselines, such as Gemini 3 Pro, across multiple downstream tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. We show that the model combines latent information with general physical understanding to predict complex properties and can be "steered" by identifying physically meaningful directions in the latent space. This allows for explicit physical manipulation and natural language interpretation of latent structures. While our experiments focus on astrophysics, the framework is domain-agnostic and applicable to various scientific fields. Our main contribution is a general framework for using LLMs as interpretable interfaces to scientific latent spaces, enabling a single model to perform diverse tasks through natural language guidance. This work marks a step toward developing scientifically capable and useful LLMs.

papers.title: Momentum Point-Perplexity Mechanics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we define forces, energies, and a principle of least action that govern hidden-state evolution in transformers? Can these laws support principled monitoring and low-risk control of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a log-Lagrangian framework that reveals an approximately conserved energy quantity in transformer hidden state dynamics, and derives a minimal-action control method called Jacobian steering that improves output quality.
papers.conclusion: Transformers follow approximate conservation laws, and this physics perspective enables principled monitoring and control for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Energy (Et = 1/2 ∥vt∥^2 * PPLt) is approximately conserved during inference across 20 transformer models.
Random-weight models conserve energy more tightly than pre-trained models.
Training shifts models into a kinetic-dominated regime with higher energy variability.
Jacobian steering, derived from the log-Lagrangian, can control generation while preserving semantic quality.
Steering improves the semantic quality of output distributions, especially for smaller models.
papers.limitation: Results cover models up to 3B parameters with English tokenizers; scaling to larger models and multilingual settings remains untested.
future_direction: Explore whether conservation laws can guide the design of inherently safer architectures and training procedures that preserve beneficial invariants.
Energy-aware monitoring, robust steering, and physics-inspired design of future models.
papers.abstract: We take a physics-based approach to studying how the internal hidden states of large language models change from token to token during inference. Across 20 open-source transformer models (135M-3B parameters), we find that a quantity combining the rate of change in hidden states and the model's next-token certainty, analogous to energy in physics, remains nearly constant. Random-weight models conserve this "energy" more tightly than pre-trained ones, while training shifts models into a faster, more decisive regime with greater variability. Using this "log-Lagrangian" view, we derive a control method called Jacobian steering, which perturbs hidden states in the minimal way needed to favor a target token. This approach maintained near-constant energy in two tested models and produced continuations rated higher in semantic quality than the models' natural outputs. Viewing transformers through this mechanics lens offers a principled basis for interpretability, anomaly detection, and low-risk steering.
